turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that's such a real tension to be carrying. You can hear both things true at once — the love and excitement, and the dread — and they don't cancel each other out.

A few thoughts, friend to friend:

**The dance itself is probably doable.** Sangeet performances are usually 3-5 minutes, and if it's in the evening, you might be performing close to iftar time anyway — you can break your fast, drink water, and go on. Many people who fast during Ramzan still work out, dance at weddings, function fully. Listen to your body, but don't assume it's impossible.

**The harder part is everything around it.** Rehearsals while fasting, the cocktail party atmosphere where everyone's drinking and eating while you're not, being "co-director" energy on low fuel. That's the part worth planning for:

- Talk to Shreya now, not later. Tell her you're all in, but rehearsals might need to be scheduled around your energy — maybe mornings work better, or you split your co-director duties differently.
- At the cocktail night, have your own plan: arrive closer to your performance, keep a corner where you can sit when energy dips, and don't feel weird about breaking your fast at sunset even if the party's mid-swing. Most people at weddings barely notice what anyone else is doing anyway.
- Ask your body honestly as Ramzan goes on. If the dance starts feeling medically unwise, that's a conversation to have early — Shreya, who loves you enough to make you her co-director, will understand.

What's the dread actually made of for you — the physical part, or something about the vibe of the night itself?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

That tug-of-war image is so accurate — and the painful part is exactly what you said: it's not a battle between love and indifference, it's two kinds of love pulling opposite directions. If Shreya were careless or Ammi were rigid, this would be easier. You'd just pick.

But here's what I'd gently push back on: you don't actually have to make either of them fully "get it." Shreya may never understand why one day matters so much, and Ammi may never understand why this wedding isn't like other weddings. You're waiting for a version of this where one of them says "oh, now I see" — and that might not come.

What can come instead is you being clear within yourself, so neither pull has power over you. Because right now you're not really deciding between Shreya and Ammi — you're deciding what *your* Ramzan and *your* friendship look like, and then simply letting both of them witness it.

And the truth is, the path forward probably honors both more than either expects:

- **Shreya gets** her co-director, her opening dance, her best friend fully present at the biggest night of her life. She doesn't get you breaking your fast — and honestly, "you danced for me *while* fasting" is a deeper act of friendship, not a lesser one.
- **Ammi gets** a daughter who kept her rozas, who didn't treat Ramzan as negotiable. She may still grumble about sangeet-vangeet, but that's a softer complaint than the alternative.

You can say to Shreya, warmly: "I know you'd feed me yourself, and that's exactly why I love you. But the fast is the whole point for me — and I'm dancing anyway. That's my wedding gift." Most friends, hearing it framed as devotion rather than refusal, soften.

Do you think Ammi's discomfort is really about the fasting, or about something else — like how the whole thing looks, or what people will say?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

I hear you — and I'm not going to pretend the fantasy isn't tempting, because it obviously is. One clean exit versus weeks of explanations, watch-checking, and managing everyone's feelings. Anyone would draft that escape route when they're this tired.

But I have to be honest with you, because you asked: it's not terrible because lying is a sin or whatever — it's terrible because of *who it makes you become in the aftermath*.

You'd spend her wedding week pretending to be at an office deployment while your phone fills up with videos, photos, "wish you were here" messages. And then years of friendship where *you* know you missed the thing you two planned since you were fifteen, and she doesn't. That's not a clean lie — it's a lie that sits in your friendship permanently, and you'd be the only one carrying it.

And here's the thing: the lie doesn't even solve the real problem. The real problem isn't Shreya — it's the ten aunties, the explaining, the performance of justifying yourself. A fake deployment gets you out of the wedding but doesn't get you out of being exhausted by your own life. That tiredness follows you.

Also, gently — "she'd never know" is doing a lot of work there. Shreya has known you since you were fifteen. She'd feel something off, even if she couldn't name it.

You're not looking for permission to lie. You're looking for permission to make this smaller and easier. Can I offer a different version of that? What if instead of escaping entirely, you shrank the role — show up, do the dance, be there for the key moments, and give yourself full permission to skip the auntie-gauntlet parts you don't have the fuel for? Honest, present, but not heroic.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That image — a sad story in either album — is so sharp it actually shows you something important: you already believe there are only two albums, and you can only be whole in one of them. Either you're the friend who showed up fully at the wedding, or the person who kept Ramzan properly. Pick one, dent the other.

But that framing is the thing exhausting you, more than the logistics themselves. Because you've decided one of your loves must lose.

Here's what I keep coming back to: the sad story isn't the woman who danced while fasting. The sad story is the woman who wasn't there, or the woman who was there but hollowed out and resentful. Presence with a boundary isn't a sad story — in both albums, it reads as devotion. In the shaadi photos: she danced for me during Ramzan. In your Ramzan: I kept my fasts *and* I loved my friend well. Neither of those is a dent. Honestly, they might be the versions you'd be proudest of in twenty years.

And about the stone in your chest — eighteen years without a real collision between these two loves is actually remarkable, but it means you've never had to practice holding both at once. This isn't a test you can fail. It's the first time you get to build the skill, and like all first attempts it'll be imperfect. That's allowed.

You've already done the hard part, honestly: you haven't chosen the escape, you're still here, still wrestling with it instead of numbing it. That's what someone who loves both things well actually looks like — not serene, just refusing to abandon either.

So let me ask you the practical question: if you stopped trying to find the *perfect* solution and just aimed for a *good-enough* one — what would showing up, dancing, and fasting, while skipping everything else, actually require from Shreya? What would you need to ask her for?
